faq.a: They are cheap, rapid, and quantitative, allowing easy monitoring of disease activity.
faq.q: Why are nontreponemal tests used for screening?

faq.a: Very high antibody concentrations can inhibit lattice formation, giving a false‑negative result; diluting the serum resolves it.
Not in very early primary disease or in late latent infection with low titres; repeat testing or use treponemal test if suspicion persists.
faq.q: Can a negative RPR rule out syphilis?

exam: A 28‑year‑old man presents with a painless genital ulcer; RPR is non‑reactive. What is your next step? — Consider the window period; obtain dark‑field microscopy or repeat RPR in 1 week.
A pregnant woman’s VDRL is 1:64. How do you interpret the titre and manage? — High titre suggests active infection; give benzathine penicillin and arrange partner treatment.
Why might a patient with systemic lupus have a reactive VDRL but no syphilis? — Anticardiolipin antibodies in lupus cause false‑positive nontreponemal test; confirm with treponemal assay.
Your patient’s RPR falls from 1:32 to 1:8 after treatment. What does this indicate? — A four‑fold decline shows adequate therapeutic response.
Explain the prozone effect and how you would detect it in the lab. — Dilute serum serially; a previously negative sample becomes positive at dilution.
In a resource‑limited clinic without VDRL kits, what alternative can you use to screen for syphilis? — Perform a rapid point‑of‑care treponemal test, acknowledging it cannot monitor treatment.
A patient with HIV has a low‑titre positive RPR (1:2). How do you decide if treatment is needed? — Correlate with clinical stage and confirm with treponemal test; treat if evidence of active disease.
What are the red‑flag signs that would prompt urgent referral in a syphilis patient? — Neurologic signs, cardiac murmurs, or pregnancy with positive test require immediate specialist input.
ai.title: Nontreponemal Tests for Syphilis
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Nontreponemal tests (RPR and VDRL) detect antibodies to cardiolipin released during syphilis infection. They are cheap, rapid, and useful for screening and monitoring treatment, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Screening tool for all patients with suspected syphilis
Quantitative titres help assess disease activity and response to therapy
sections.p: Nontreponemal tests are serologic assays that detect IgG/IgM antibodies directed against cardiolipin‑lecithin‑cholesterol antigen complexes released from damaged host cells, not against Treponema pallidum itself.

t.b: Is the patient currently infected or have active disease? – A reactive result indicates presence of anticardiolipin antibodies; titre magnitude correlates with activity.
Same question as RPR; used when laboratory infrastructure allows flocculation method – reactive result similar interpretation.

b: Primary: usually low or negative titres
Secondary: high titres, often ≥1:32
Late latent: low titres, often ≤1:8
sections.p: Nontreponemal titres rise in primary and secondary syphilis and fall after effective treatment. Very high titres (≥1:32) suggest secondary disease; low titres (≤1:4) may indicate late latent or treated infection.

b: Syphilis (any stage) – most common cause
Pregnancy, HIV infection, malaria, TB, hepatitis B
Autoimmune diseases (SLE, rheumatoid arthritis)
Recent viral infections, intravenous drug use, certain antibiotics
sections.p: The test is positive when the host produces anticardiolipin antibodies, most commonly due to active syphilis infection. False‑positives arise from other conditions.

b: Painless genital ulcer (primary)
Maculopapular rash including palms/soles (secondary)
Neurologic or cardiac symptoms in late disease
sections.p: Patients present with signs of syphilis (chancre, rash, mucous patches) or with nonspecific complaints prompting routine screening (antenatal visit, HIV clinic).

b: If RPR/VDRL unavailable, use dark‑field microscopy of lesion exudate where feasible
sections.p: Nontreponemal tests are the first line; positive results must be confirmed with a treponemal test (e.g., TPHA, FTA‑ABS).

t.b: Screening – does the patient have antibodies suggestive of syphilis? – Reactive = positive; non‑reactive = unlikely active infection.
Confirmatory – does the patient have antibodies specific to T. pallidum? – Positive confirms infection regardless of stage.
Monitoring – is treatment effective? – Four‑fold decline (e.g., 1:32 to 1:8) by 6‑12 months indicates adequate response.

b: Persistent high titres despite therapy
Neurologic signs (headache, cranial nerve palsy)
Aortic aneurysm or valvular disease
Pregnant woman with positive test – risk of fetal infection
sections.p: Untreated syphilis can progress to neurosyphilis, cardiovascular syphilis, or congenital infection.

b: First‑line: Benzathine penicillin G (single dose for early disease, weekly for 3 weeks for late latent).
Avoid macrolides in areas with high macrolide‑resistant T. pallidum.
sections.p: Treat the underlying Treponema infection; nontreponemal tests guide when to start and when to stop therapy.

b: Four‑fold titre fall = successful treatment
No decline or rise = treatment failure or reinfection
Vaccination not available – rely on screening and education
sections.p: Repeat quantitative RPR at 6 months (early disease) or 12 months (late disease). Counsel on safe sex and partner notification.

b: False‑positive VDRL in lupus vs true syphilis
Prozone phenomenon – very high antibody levels can give false‑negative result
sections.p: Treponemal tests (TPHA, FTA‑ABS) detect antibodies specific to T. pallidum and remain positive for life, unlike nontreponemal tests which can revert to non‑reactive after cure.

b: Prozone: dilute sample to uncover hidden positivity
Early primary syphilis may be non‑reactive – repeat testing after 1 week if suspicion remains
sections.p: False‑positive nontreponemal tests occur in many conditions; false‑negative results can happen early (window period) or with the prozone effect.

whenToSeekHelp: Neurologic deficits, severe headache, or visual changes (possible neurosyphilis)
Chest pain or dyspnoea with aortic murmur (cardiovascular syphilis)
Pregnant woman with positive test – urgent obstetric referral
